Was Muʿāwiya, from an objective historical point of view, actually wrong to do what he did?

I believe that a state with the historical weight of the Arab-Umayyad state could hardly have become stable, put down firm roots, and played its historical role if Muʿāwiya had not supported it with this bold political measure.
We also need to consider the fact that Yazīd himself happened to be the first man who would inherit Muʿāwiya’s throne under this new hereditary system.

It helped deepen the widespread resentment caused by Muʿāwiya’s change to the caliphate. It also helped give the Shiʿi uprising—and al-Ḥusayn’s death while fighting Yazīd’s army—a lasting presence in public life, political movements, and intellectual history.
Choosing Yazīd as the first heir gave the opponents of hereditary rule a powerful argument against the whole principle. It gave them a practical weapon with which to attack it.

The issue could no longer be limited to the Shiʿi claim that the caliphate was a divine right belonging to ʿAlī and his sons. It now reached the Sunnis as well. They believed that the caliphate belonged to the Muslim community, which should choose whoever was best qualified to carry its heavy responsibilities.
And Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya had none of the qualities that would make him “the best qualified.”
First, he was a young man whose conduct and way of life were widely criticized.
Second, he was known for disregarding even basic standards of behavior and religious observance.

Third, he knew little about how to manage the public affairs of a state. Between Yazīd and the responsibilities he had been given stood a thick wall of isolation, together with his constant absorption in trivial daily amusements.
We should add a fourth point. People at the time may not yet have understood it clearly as a social issue, but that does not make it any less real.

Yazīd’s character and behavior were typical of the young men of the new aristocratic class. They looked down on ordinary people and immersed themselves in shallow material luxury. Their way of life separated them from the serious problems and everyday struggles that occupied the great majority of people.
This must have affected how people felt about them, even if that feeling had not yet developed into a clear social awareness.
The first two factors pushed Muslims, especially after the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, toward an increasingly negative comparison, whether they made it consciously or simply felt it.
It was a comparison between two men.
On one side stood Yazīd, with the character we have just described.

On the other stood al-Ḥusayn. Muslims knew that he was the grandson of the Prophet, the son of Muḥammad’s daughter. They knew that his father was ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, one of the Rightly Guided caliphs, whom Muslims in general regarded with great respect. They also knew al-Ḥusayn for his own personal qualities, and they knew that he had courageously accepted a tragic fate while defending what he believed to be his right.
The comparison left many Muslims with a deep sense of grief.

They grieved not only because of al-Ḥusayn’s terrible fate, but also because an army acting in the name of the Umayyad caliphate had killed him; because of the shocking way in which the killing had taken place; and because the Islamic caliphate itself now seemed to be passing into the hands of men of bloodshed who had opened their new era with an event of such horror.

A modern scholar of the Ashʿarī school, far removed from Shiʿi emotional attachment to the event, says that Muslims had never seen anything like it. He says that Muslims as a whole cursed Yazīd because of the massacre of 61 AH. This modern Ashʿarī scholar even describes the killing of al-Ḥusayn as “the greatest event in the political and spiritual history of Islam.”
Together, these three factors, and others like them, helped the Shiʿi uprising continue far beyond Karbala.

At times it took the form of bloody uprisings and revolts. These began with the revolt of al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī, after the revolt of the Tawwābūn, or Penitents. The revolt of the Penitents was a direct and violent expression of the remorse felt by the people of Kufa for failing to support al-Ḥusayn in his struggle against Yazīd’s army. It was also, less directly, an expression of the effect that the factors we have just discussed had left on Muslim society.

At other times, the same Shiʿi uprising appeared in the form of intellectual movements. At first these took a purely religious form. Later they developed theological and philosophical forms as well, as we will see in the next chapter.

We should add that many of the Companions of the Prophet and the generation that followed them in Medina had their own particular reasons for resenting Muʿāwiya’s hereditary system. The same was true in Mecca.

These were the two holy cities of Islam. Their people saw themselves as closely tied to Islam because they had personally nurtured its cause through their own lives and sacrifices. Islam had grown up among them and had remained closely connected with their lives.
For that reason, they were especially sensitive to anything they believed threatened it.

Some of them regarded Muʿāwiya’s transformation of the caliphate away from the model of the Rightly Guided caliphs as an innovation in Islam. In their view, it did not merely go against the practice of the early caliphs. More importantly, it went against the basic nature of the caliphate itself, as we have already explained.

Then there were the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. They denied not only Muʿāwiya’s right to the caliphate, but even the right of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. They believed that the caliphate was a divine office whose holder had to be named by God through the Prophet, and that such a designation had already been made in favor of ʿAlī immediately after the Prophet.
These were two religiously based positions toward Muʿāwiya’s caliphate that existed in Medina.
But there were other reasons for dissatisfaction as well. Some were personal and political. Others were social and class-based.
The first kind came from the ambitions of some of the sons of the Companions, such as Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr and his brother ʿAbd Allāh, who themselves hoped to become caliph.
The second kind came from the transfer of the center of the caliphate from Medina to Damascus.

This move cost Medina its almost central position in the Arab-Islamic world. It also cost the wealthy people of Medina, and those of Mecca, many of the benefits they had gained from that position. Their economic and political activity declined. Many of their ambitions were blocked. They found themselves pushed almost entirely away from the center of political and social life.

Several things had prevented Medina from rising against Muʿāwiya while he was alive: his wealth and political skill, the conflict between ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya, and the decision of many of the leading men we have mentioned to side against ʿAlī.
But as soon as Muʿāwiya’s son Yazīd inherited the Umayyad throne in Damascus, the resentment that had previously been held back began to move toward open revolt.
Again, Yazīd’s own character mattered greatly. The qualities we described earlier helped turn resentment into an explosion.
Yazīd was therefore left with little support except from those who had a direct interest in keeping him as ruler of the Muslims in Damascus—and, more broadly, in preserving the Umayyad throne itself.
These were, on the one hand, the representatives of the ruling class in Syria and, on the other, the Kalb tribes, who were allied with the Umayyads there.

Everything pointed toward an approaching revolt in Medina, and in Mecca as well. The wider explosion had in fact already begun after the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī in Iraq, where two movements hostile to the Umayyads were active despite their deep differences: the Shiʿa and the Khārijites.
Then the revolt came in Medina.
The people of the city openly rebelled and refused to pledge allegiance to Yazīd as caliph. Yazīd sent his Syrian army, made up of those allies, and crushed the rebellion.

His army then continued toward Mecca and placed the city under siege. During the siege, it committed an extraordinary act that shocked Muslims everywhere and continued to do so for generations: the army bombarded the Kaaba itself, along with the homes of the city’s inhabitants, and set fires around it.
Yazīd did not live long after this.

He died that same year, in 683 CE. His son, Muʿāwiya II, succeeded him, but remained caliph for only a few months and did not truly exercise power because of an illness from which he suffered. He then died of plague at the age of twenty.
With his death, the Umayyad throne passed to another branch of the family, that of Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam. Marwān became the first caliph after the three Sufyanids: Muʿāwiya I, Yazīd, and Muʿāwiya II.
Mecca experienced another of the major upheavals of the Umayyad period when ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr emerged as a claimant to the caliphate after the death of Muʿāwiya II.

His father, al-Zubayr, had been one of the leading Companions of the Prophet. As we saw earlier, he later fought against ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib in the Battle of the Camel at Basra. Together with ʿĀʾisha, he entered that war demanding revenge for the killing of the third caliph, ʿUthmān, and he was killed in the course of those events.
Now his son ʿAbd Allāh appeared in the Hijaz and declared himself caliph.

He saw that the Umayyad throne in Damascus had been shaken since the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī in Iraq. Then, after the deaths of Yazīd and his son Muʿāwiya II, the dynasty itself seemed in danger of disappearing.

The opportunity had arrived for these ambitious sons of the Companions, whom Muʿāwiya I had pushed away from the center of Arab-Islamic political life when he established the Umayyad caliphate in Syria, far from Mecca and Medina, the earlier centers of Arab and Muslim life.

These young men saw themselves as natural candidates for power because they came from the leading families of both Mecca and Medina. They even believed that they had a stronger claim than the descendants of Abū Sufyān, who had once fought against the Prophet and Islam while their own fathers had been among the Prophet’s leading Companions.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr now rose up in an attempt to return the caliphate to its original home in the Hijaz.
In doing so, he made use of the same old tribal rivalry that Muʿāwiya had previously exploited: the conflict between the Qays tribes and the Kalb tribes.

The Qays tribes, for their part, saw Ibn al-Zubayr’s movement as an opportunity to defeat the Kalb tribes and take from them the positions of power they had gained through their long alliance with Muʿāwiya.

Muʿāwiya was now gone, and the throne he had built seemed close to collapse. The Qays tribes therefore had every reason to move quickly, support ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, and recognize him as caliph before a new Umayyad leader appeared in Syria and took the opportunity away from them.
The Qays-Kalb conflict thus erupted again.
The two sides met at the Battle of Marj Rāhiṭ near Damascus. It was a major battle, and the Kalb tribes won an overwhelming victory.
Then the new Umayyad leader whom the Qays tribes had feared finally appeared: Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam.
The Kalb tribes recognized him as the new caliph on the Umayyad throne in Damascus, a throne they themselves had helped save from collapse.
But ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr was not defeated simply because the Qays tribes had lost at Marj Rāhiṭ. Other Arab tribes in Iraq and Iran still supported him against the Umayyads.

At the same time, the supporters of ʿAlī were in no position to mount serious resistance to the Umayyads after the massacre at Karbala, and no Alid leader had yet emerged to lead a revolt against Umayyad rule.
Ibn al-Zubayr therefore still had enough support to maintain his claim to the caliphate in Mecca, where he had already taken control.
Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam, meanwhile, held power in Damascus.
Besides the Kalb tribes, he had the support of the wealthy class that controlled the great fortunes and large estates, and he himself was one of its representatives.

During the rule of the Rightly Guided caliph ʿUthmān, Marwān had already helped the Umayyads gain control over wealth and property and concentrate it in their own hands. His actions were also among the causes of the revolt against ʿUthmān.
Marwān had served as ʿUthmān’s secretary and exercised great influence over him. Some historians even describe him as the real ruler during that period.
This makes it easier to see how the political and social character of Umayyad rule continued under Marwān just as it had under its founder, Muʿāwiya.

Marwān did not appear merely as the man who saved Umayyad rule. He also came to protect the privileges of the wealthy, the great landowners, the leading Umayyads, and their allies—in other words, the local wealthy class and the Kalb tribes.
But Marwān did not rule for long.
His wife strangled him out of jealousy over one of his favored slave women. His son ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān then succeeded him on the Umayyad throne.

When ʿAbd al-Malik came to power, he faced two powerful movements that threatened his control over the Hijaz, Iraq, and Iran: the movement of ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, who ruled Mecca, and the Khārijite movement.

There was also the revolt of al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī in Iraq. Al-Mukhtār had risen to avenge the blood of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī and was hunting down those who had taken part in his killing in order to destroy them physically.
But Ibn al-Zubayr’s movement posed the greatest danger to the Umayyad caliphate. ʿAbd al-Malik therefore had to deal with that threat first.

Despite the strong position Ibn al-Zubayr had gained by attracting many of the forces opposed to the Umayyads, he does not seem to have had enough political skill or foresight to make good use of that support or even to keep it.
He committed acts that deeply offended believers, much as Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya had done earlier when his army bombarded the Kaaba with catapults.
Ibn al-Zubayr ruled harshly and despotically. At the same time, while sitting in the Kaaba itself, he openly expressed irreligious views and contempt for religion.
Because of this, he could not withstand the Umayyad army that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān sent to Mecca to bring him under control.
His own supporters deserted him because of the way he had behaved. By the time the Umayyad army arrived, he was already badly weakened.
He tried to take refuge in the Kaaba, but his mother, Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, encouraged him to face the Umayyads directly.
He went out to fight them in the streets of Mecca. Before long he was killed, and ʿAbd al-Malik’s army won the victory.
ʿAbd al-Malik then had to deal with the burning problems of opposition in Iraq.

There were the Khārijites and the Shiʿa. The Khārijites were disturbing the security of the Umayyad state. The Shiʿa were spreading ideas and an “ideology” hostile to the Umayyads, while their ally al-Mukhtār ibn Abī ʿUbayd al-Thaqafī was using armed force to kill everyone who had taken part in the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī.
The Umayyad governor of Iraq had also sided with Ibn al-Zubayr and then adopted positions that supported all the opposition forces, including both the Khārijites and the Shiʿa.
At this point al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf al-Thaqafī enters the story. We will return to him when we discuss the Khārijites.
This time, the Umayyad throne, under ʿAbd al-Malik himself, faced a new kind of class uprising.
First, it came from inside the Umayyads’ own secure stronghold: Syria itself.
Second, it came from deep within society, from one of its poorest, most oppressed groups: the slaves.

The slaves of Damascus rose in rebellion. They went to the prisons and released everyone being held there. The slaves and the freed prisoners then withdrew to the mountain overlooking Damascus and took shelter there.
